bib.title: Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug", Xinyun Chen, Maxwell Lin, Nathanael Schärli, Denny Zhou (Google DeepMind; UC Berkeley). The PDF is arXiv:2304.05128v2, dated 5 Oct 2023. The extracted text has no ICLR line. "ICLR 2024" comes from the brief, not from this file.

File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/04-loop-engineering/sources/chen-2023-teaching-large-language-models-self.pdf

COVERAGE: 78 pages, 193,614 chars.
- **Read in full:** pp. 1–14 (body and conclusion), Appendix A–D on pp. 19–22 (Tables 5–6, Figs 8–11), and every chat prompt: E.6–E.7 (p. 54), F.7–F.10 (pp. 63–65), G.5–G.8 (pp. 76–78).
- **Skimmed:** references on pp. 14–19, for origins only. The few-shot prompts E.1–E.5, F.1–F.6 and G.1–G.4 (pp. 23–75) are long, repetitive Spider schemas and code exemplars. I read every section header plus samples of E.1, E.2, F.1 and G.2, not every exemplar.
- **Not checked:** I did not open the target note in full. I only grepped it. It does not cite this paper yet. Its nearest related point is at line 223: "Reflexion-style self-reflection can *propose* lessons, but reflection is not evidence."

CLAIMS (ranked)

- claim: With unit-test execution feedback, self-debugging lifts TransCoder (C++ to Python) accuracy by about 12 points for Codex and GPT-4.
  number: Codex 80.4 → 92.5 (UT + Expl.); GPT-4 77.3 → 90.4
  setup: TransCoder test set (560 problems, 10 unit tests each, all visible in the prompt). Debugging runs only when a unit test fails. Greedy decoding. At most 10 turns.
  quote: "TransCoder Codex GPT-3.5 GPT-4 StarCoder Baseline 80.4 89.1 77.3 70.0 ... UT 91.6 92.7 88.8 76.4 + Expl. 92.5 92.7 90.4 76.6" and "over 12% improvement on Transcoder, and 8% improvement on MBPP."
  where: Table 2b, p. 9; text p. 9

- claim: On MBPP (one unit test visible, two hidden), self-debugging adds about 8 points for GPT-4 and smaller gains for the other models.
  number: GPT-4 72.8 → 80.6 (UT); Codex 61.4 → 70.8 (+Trace); StarCoder 47.2 → 53.2
  setup: 500 MBPP test problems. The first test goes in the prompt and the other 2 are held out for scoring.
  quote: "MBPP Codex GPT-3.5 GPT-4 StarCoder Baseline 61.4 67.6 72.8 47.2 Simple 68.2 70.8 78.8 50.6 UT 69.4 72.2 80.6 52.2 + Expl. 69.8 74.2 80.4 52.2 + Trace. 70.8 72.8 80.2 53.2"
  where: Table 2c, p. 9

- claim: On Spider (no unit tests), simple "is it correct?" feedback does nothing, because the model cannot tell right SQL from wrong. Code explanation adds about 3 points, but only for Codex.
  number: Codex 81.3 → 84.1 (+Expl.); GPT-3.5 71.1 → 72.2; GPT-4 73.2 → 73.6; StarCoder 64.7 → 64.9
  setup: Spider dev set. The model sees the executed SQL's returned table (first 2 rows) plus its own explanation. So execution results are present, but there is no correctness oracle.
  quote: "Spider Codex GPT-3.5 GPT-4 StarCoder Baseline 81.3 71.1 73.2 64.7 Simple 81.3 72.2 73.4 64.9 +Expl. 84.1 72.2 73.6 64.9" and "simple feedback alone does not notably improve the performance, because the model typically struggles to distinguish between correct and wrong SQL queries without explanation"
  where: Table 2a, p. 9; pp. 7–8

- claim: Without unit-test execution, gains shrink to between about −4 and +5 points, and simple self-feedback can hurt. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 tend to be overconfident in their first answer.
  number: MBPP Codex Simple 61.4 → 57.6 (a drop); Codex +Trace 66.2; GPT-4 72.8 → 76.4; TransCoder GPT-3.5 89.1 under every feedback type
  setup: TransCoder and MBPP with code execution removed. The model alone judges correctness.
  quote: "MBPP Codex GPT-3.5 GPT-4 Baseline 61.4 67.6 72.8 Simple 57.6 68.2 76.0 + Expl. 64.4 68.2 76.0 + Trace. 66.2 69.2 76.4" and "Without unit test execution, both models tend to be overconfident in their own initial predictions" and "code execution plays an important role in SELF -D EBUGGING ; however, sometimes LLMs can still improve their performance purely with self-generated feedback."
  where: Table 3, p. 10

- claim: Self-debugging is more sample-efficient than drawing more candidates and majority-voting. On Spider, debugging one greedy sample matches the 16-sample baseline, and debugging 8 samples beats the 32-sample baseline.
  number: baseline 77.5/78.7/80.7/81.3 at 1/8/16/32 samples; with self-debugging 80.8/82.5/82.9/84.1
  setup: Spider dev, Codex. Samples drawn at τ=0.7 and chosen by execution-based majority vote.
  quote: "applying SELF -D EBUGGING to predictions generated with greedy decoding matches the baseline accuracy using 16 samples, andSELF -D EBUGGING from 8 samples outperforms the baseline accuracy using 32 samples."
  where: Fig. 6a, p. 10

- claim: The abstract's "matches >10× samples" claim is backed by the TransCoder sample curve.
  number: 10×
  setup: TransCoder, Codex, greedy decoding plus debugging, compared with 5 and 10 samples.
  quote: "applying SELF -D EBUGGING to greedy decoding outperforms the baseline accuracy with 5 samples, and is close to the baseline accuracy with 10 samples." (abstract: "can match or outperform baseline models that generate more than 10× candidate programs.")
  where: App. C.1, p. 20; abstract p. 1

- claim: Most of the gain comes in the first debugging turn.
  number: TransCoder UT+Expl. 80.4 → about 91–92 after turn 1, 92.5 by turn 3; Spider gain after turn 1 within 0.1%
  setup: maximum 10 turns allowed
  quote: "We set the maximum number of debugging turns to be 10, though empirically the successful debugging processes mostly end within 3 turns." / "typically one debugging turn is sufficient, and the accuracy improvement after one turn is within 0.1%." / "a single debugging turn with the full feedback improves over the greedy decoding accuracy by around 12%."
  where: p. 7; p. 10; p. 20 (Fig. 8a)

- claim: Self-debugging helps most on hard problems.
  number: extra-hard Spider 63.9 → 72.9 (+9); easy 90.7 → 92.3
  setup: Spider dev, Codex
  quote: "on extra hard problems, SELF -DEBUGGING increases the accuracy by 9%."
  where: Fig. 6b, p. 11

- claim: Code explanation alone, with no debugging loop, gives 2–3 points on TransCoder.
  number: 2–3%
  setup: TransCoder, Codex+Expl. (the model only explains the input C++), measured across sample counts
  quote: "leveraging code explanation alone without SELF -D EBUGGING also provides a consistent performance gain of 2 − 3% for different numbers of samples"
  where: p. 20, Fig. 8b

- claim: The fixed errors are mostly small near-misses: output mismatches and runtime errors in code, wrong WHERE clauses and missing DISTINCT in SQL.
  number: Output mismatch 61.9 (TransCoder) / 69.2 (MBPP); WHERE 25.7%; DISTINCT 17.1%
  setup: successful fixes only. Spider uses Codex, TransCoder uses GPT-3.5, MBPP uses GPT-4.
  quote: "60%-70% successful cases fix the output mismatch error when the initial wrong code is very close to a correct one"
  where: Table 4, p. 12

- claim: State of the art at the time. Prompting alone beats trained rerankers on Spider and MBPP, using fewer samples.
  number: Spider 84.1 vs LEVER 81.9 and T5-3B reranking 80.6; MBPP 75.6 (n=10) vs LEVER 68.9 (n=100); TransCoder pass@1 92.5 vs PaLM-Coder 55.1
  quote: "Codex 72.2 ( n = 10) Simple 73.6 UT 75.2 UT + Expl. 75.6" ; "LEVER 68.9 ( n = 100)"
  where: Table 1, p. 9; Table 6, p. 19

- claim: Few-shot debugging prompts favour Codex. GPT-4 does worse than Codex on few-shot Spider, which the authors attribute to tuning for zero-shot use.
  quote: "One possible reason is that GPT-4 is tuned for zero-shot prompting, and thus it does not follow few-shot exemplars as well as Codex."
  where: p. 9

LIMITS
- **No cost accounting.** "Sample efficiency" counts candidate programs, not tokens or calls. Each debugging turn adds prompts for explanation and feedback, and those tokens are never compared.
- **Single runs.** Results are greedy single runs with no variance, seeds or confidence intervals. Many differences are 0.2–1 point.
- **Spider still uses execution.** The "no unit tests" setting still feeds the executed result table to the model, so it is not a pure self-explanation test.
- **The case without execution is weak and mixed.** Table 3 shows near-zero gains for GPT-3.5 and a 3.8-point drop for Codex with simple feedback on MBPP.
- **The MBPP protocol limits harm.** In the chat prompts (G.5–G.7), once code passes the visible test, one "Is the code above correct?" round runs, and "The new code prediction is used only if it also passes the unit test." The visible test therefore guards against regressions.
- **Explanation helps less on MBPP.** The authors give three reasons: unit tests already flag errors, explanation prompts have fewer exemplars (3 vs 6) because of context length, and explanation helps little when the first code is far from correct (p. 20).
- **Conceded by the authors:** "model-generated feedback messages about semantic errors do not provide additional benefits on top of line-by-line code explanation" (p. 14). They also note that GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 gain little from few-shot prompting.
- **Dated.** The models are code-davinci-002, gpt-3.5-turbo, early GPT-4 and StarCoder-15.5B. Codex has been deprecated. The benchmarks are short-function tasks, not repo-scale or agentic coding.

BUILDS ON
- Rubber duck debugging: Hunt & Thomas, 2000.
- Execution-based selection and majority vote: Chen et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2022 (MBR-Exec).
- Reranking: Zhang et al., 2022 (Coder-Reviewer); Ni et al., 2023 (LEVER).
- Trained code repair: Gupta et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018 (execution traces); Yasunaga & Liang, 2020/2021; Le et al., 2022.
- Code repair from human feedback: Chen et al., 2023a, the prior finding that LLMs "are not yet capable of correcting code when lacking external feedback".
- Prompted self-critique: Shinn et al., 2023 (Reflexion); Madaan et al., 2023b (Self-Refine); Kim et al., 2023 (RCI); Nair et al., 2023 (DERA); Bai et al., 2022 (Constitutional AI).
- Chain-of-thought: Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022.

CODE
The simple feedback strings (p. 3): “The SQL prediction above is correct!” / “The SQL prediction above is wrong. Please fix the SQL.”

The MBPP chat loop with unit-test feedback (App. G.6, pp. 76–77), verbatim:
```
User: The code above fails the given unit test:
<insert the failed unit test and its execution result here>
Please fix the Python code.
...
User: Is the code above correct? If not, please fix it.
Assistant: <chatGPT Completion>
The new code prediction is used only if it also passes the unit test, otherwise the original code will be used for evaluation.
```

FIGURES
- **Fig. 1, p. 2.** The loop: generation → execution → explanation → feedback. It shows the loop structure faster than prose.
- **Fig. 5, p. 8.** The four feedback types side by side (Simple, UT, UT+Expl., UT+Trace) on one `n / i` float bug. It makes the ablation's levels concrete.
- **Fig. 6, p. 10.** (a) Spider accuracy against number of samples, with and without self-debugging; this is the cleanest picture of debugging versus sampling more. (b) Accuracy by difficulty level.
- **Fig. 8, p. 20.** (a) TransCoder accuracy by turn, which shows returns flattening after turn 1. (b) Accuracy by sample count, including explanation without debugging.
- **Fig. 3, p. 6.** A worked SQL self-debug over two revisions (OR → AND → INTERSECT). Good for one illustrative example.
- **Tables 2 and 3 (pp. 9–10) are not figures,** but together they show the main point: with execution feedback against without it.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions aimed at the reader. The appendix contains the paper's own prompt templates ("System: You are an expert programming assistant."), which are study material.
- Small caps break words in the extraction ("SELF -D EBUGGING"). Some tables lost their column alignment; I rebuilt them from the order of headers and values.
- Fig. 8a values are extracted out of order (80.4, 88.4, 89.3, 91.1, 91.6, 92.0, 92.5 across 3 series), so per-series values by turn are uncertain. Only 80.4 (turn 0) and 92.5 (UT+Expl. final) are certain.
- The venue cannot be confirmed from this PDF: it is the arXiv v2 preprint.
